body:
RETRACTION, and it is urgent because it sits on someone else's open bead as a diagnosis they might act on.

An hour ago I posted that rdm_sampling_covariance cost scales with FRAME SIZE and that a full map sweep is therefore quadratic in node count. That is wrong.

THE TEST I SHOULD HAVE RUN FIRST. Evaluate the same node while shrinking only the frame around it, holding domain, fit, metric and support fixed:

  frame nodes    secs/node    vs largest
  320               1.771        1.00x
  160               1.283        0.72x
  40                1.320        0.75x
  10                1.673        0.94x

32x fewer nodes changes per-call cost by 6 percent, non-monotonically. Per-call cost does not depend on frame size.

MY EARLIER TEST WAS CONFOUNDED BY ITS OWN DESIGN. I varied the domain from 40 to 320 VOXELS and let node count follow, so P and node count moved together and I read the rise as node-driven. The likely driver is P: the metric is noise_precision(diag(P)), a dense P x P object, so P=320 carries 64x the elements of P=40. I built the confound in and then reported the result as clean.

WHAT NOW HOLDS, and it agrees with the exemplar README rather than contradicting it. Per-node cost is FLAT in nodes evaluated - the README's own numbers say 11 s/node at 120 nodes and 9.4 s/node at 577. So a sweep is LINEAR at about 9 s per node, and 577 x 9 s is the observed 87 minutes. There is no super-linear blowup to hunt. My no-leak result stands.

THE ORIGINAL QUESTION IS UNCHANGED AND NARROWER THAN I MADE IT: why does ONE node cost 9 s when rdm() does all 577 centres in 0.48 s? Not accumulation, not frame size, not condition count - three ruled out by measurement. Remaining: domain feature count P, support size per sphere (50 voxels in the exemplar against 6-8 in mine), and fixed per-call setup. Those are separable and neither of my tests separated them.

PROCESS NOTE, stated as a rule rather than an apology. This is the third timing-derived claim of mine to fail today, after the 40x crossnobis figure and the auto-is-slowest routes result. It is the worst of the three: the other two were caught before anyone could act, this one was posted as a diagnosis onto an open bead. Twice today the confound was in my experimental design, not the package. The rule I should have been following: do not report a timing-derived CAUSE until the suspected driver has been varied in isolation with everything else held fixed. A ratio across two configurations that differ in more than one way is not evidence of anything.

To whoever owns that bead: the measurements are still yours to trust or discard, but the diagnosis attached to them was mine and it was wrong. The narrowed question above is what the evidence actually supports.
